content.text: Electric circuits contain many different components, each with its own function and symbol. From simple switches to complex transistors, understanding what each component does and how to represent it in circuit diagrams is essential for designing, building, and troubleshooting electrical systems.
Every circuit component has a standard symbol used in circuit diagrams. You must learn to recognise and draw these symbols accurately in exams.

content.text: LEDs have largely replaced incandescent bulbs in modern lighting because they convert a much higher proportion of electrical energy into light rather than heat, making them far more energy-efficient.
"Longer line in cell symbol is negative"
— Voltmeters are always in parallel. Ammeters go in series.
— LEDs only work in forward bias. Reversed, they block current.
— Fuses protect against overcurrent but don't prevent electric shock. That requires RCDs.
— IEC (rectangle) and US (zigzag) standards differ, but both are correct.

Cell (+/- lines) connected to a switch (break in wire), then to a lamp (circle with cross). Ammeter (circle with A) in series anywhere in the loop. Voltmeter (circle with V) connected in parallel across the lamp -- wires branch off on either side of the lamp to the voltmeter.

An LED has very low resistance when forward-biased. Without a series resistor, excessive current would flow, overheating and destroying the LED. The resistor limits the current to a safe value (typically ~20 mA).
-- its resistance changes with temperature, so it can sense temperature changes.
-- connected in parallel to measure p.d. (recall)

As temperature increases, the thermistor's resistance decreases (NTC type). Since total voltage is fixed at 9 V and the two components share it, a smaller share goes to the thermistor and a larger share goes to the fixed resistor. So the p.d. across the fixed resistor increases.

An LDR is placed in series with a fixed resistor across a supply. The voltage is taken from the junction between them and fed to a buzzer or relay circuit. In normal light the LDR has low resistance, so most voltage drops across the fixed resistor. When the light beam is interrupted, the LDR's resistance rises sharply, increasing the voltage across the LDR and triggering the alarm.

A switch is a user-operated device that deliberately opens or closes a circuit -- it can be used repeatedly. A fuse is a safety device containing a thin wire that melts and permanently breaks the circuit when current exceeds its rating, protecting against overcurrent. A blown fuse must be replaced; a switch can simply be toggled.
